docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: Project OpenField is an open-source, affordable autonomous robot that marks construction layouts directly onto new home foundations. A master microcontroller coordinates four subsystems: a LiDAR board for obstacle detection, a cliff sensor board that detects drop-offs, a motor driver for precise positioning, and a spray system that marks the layout on the floor. The goal is to make construction layout faster and more accurate than marking by hand.

docs.title: Product Mission Statement
docs.text: Our mission is to build an open-source autonomous robot that accurately marks construction layouts on new home foundations, making layout work faster, cheaper, and more precise than marking by hand.

docs.title: Team Charter
docs.text:
Our team is committed to designing and developing an open‑source, reliable, and affordable autonomous robot that transforms how construction layout work is performed. We aim to create a system capable of accurately marking floor plans, assisting builders on new home foundations, and improving efficiency and precision in construction layout design.

We value accessibility, transparency, and engineering excellence. By keeping our platform open-source, we empower builders, students, and innovators to adapt, improve, and expand the robot’s capabilities. Our work emphasizes safety, durability, and real‑world usability, ensuring the robot can operate effectively in demanding construction environments.

As a team, we commit to collaboration, accountability, and continuous learning. We will communicate openly, support one another’s strengths, and uphold high standards in both technical development and project management. Our shared goal is to deliver a tool that meaningfully improves construction workflows and sets a foundation for future innovation in autonomous field robotics.

docs.title: Team Goals
docs.text:
1. Improve our understanding of mechatronics.
  2. Design a project that is simple and efficient.
  3. Discuss and learn with other engineers, gaining their perspective.
  4. Gain confidence in our ability to complete a project from start to finish.
  5. Deliver a layout robot that accurately marks floor plans on new home foundations.

docs.title: Expert Interview
docs.text: Jake Okun, Instructional Professional, School of Manufacturing Systems and Networks, Ira A. Fulton Schools of Engineering, Arizona State University. He holds degrees in Manufacturing Engineering and in Robotics and Autonomous Systems (Systems Engineering concentration), and works on wearable robotics, exoskeletons, and industrial automation.

docs.title: 1. When designing a robotics system with multiple components or modules, what are some of the biggest integration problems you have encountered?
docs.text: Response: Measurements and components not fitting together properly.

docs.title: 2. What factors do you consider when selecting components such as sensors, motors, microcontrollers, or motor drivers for a robotics project?
docs.text: Response: Power supply, dimensions, use case, customer requirements, and budget.

docs.title: 3. How important is designing a product for assembly, and what should engineers consider before they begin manufacturing a prototype?
docs.text: Response: One of the biggest considerations is tolerance and making sure everything fits together properly. Machining capabilities also need to be considered because, without specific machinery, you may not be able to manufacture the part you originally designed.

docs.title: 4. How do you decide whether a component should be 3D printed, machined, purchased, or manufactured another way?
docs.text: Response: It depends on the use case. If a stronger part is required, it should generally be machined or purchased. If an appropriate component is available off the shelf, it should be purchased. If something needs to be manufactured quickly or does not require as much strength, 3D printing can be a good option.

docs.title: 5. How do engineers handle situations where the ideal component is too expensive, unavailable, or difficult to source?
docs.text: Response: You can manufacture your own component if the existing option is too expensive or substitute it with another component. If the component is not necessary, it may also be removed entirely. There is usually an alternative solution.

docs.title: Voice of the Customer Benchmarking
docs.text: We benchmarked three existing layout robots to learn what users like and dislike about current products. We searched trade publications, contractor write-ups, dealer review pages, community discussion threads, and product datasheets. Independent user reviews of layout robots are rare because the products are new and mostly sold directly to large contractors, so we used a mix of sources and noted where a source may be biased.

docs.title: Positive Feedback

docs.title: Negative Feedback

The system marks within building-layout tolerance, not just roadwork tolerance. A single robot handles both rough ground and finished slabs. Latent Summary: The robot takes standard aerosol cans, but "the nozzle must be replaced with the standardised nozzle supplied with the robot." (Aptella datasheet) B25. Marking supplies can be replaced with standard parts. Latent Summary: Centimeter accuracy requires a GNSS receiver, and millimeter precision requires a robotic total station. (Monsen Engineering guide) B26. The robot positions itself accurately without extra survey instruments. Latent

docs.title: Benchmarking Takeaways
docs.text:
• Accuracy is the top need. Users of every product judged it first on whether the marks matched the design (B1, B13, B21). This supports our 1/16-inch tolerance need (#21).
  • Cost and ownership are the biggest complaints. HP SitePrint costs about 50,000 USD plus printing fees, and Dusty can only be rented by subscription (B6, B16). This supports our goal of an open-source, affordable robot.
  • Job-site conditions cause problems. Cold, wind, dust, ledges, and rough ground all limited current products (B8, B14, B17, B24). This supports our environmental needs and our choice of treads for traction.
  • Users want independence from expensive add-ons. Both HP and TinySurveyor need external survey equipment, and HP's supplies may be locked to one vendor (B5, B7, B25, B26).

docs.title: Section Overview
docs.text: The goal of this section was to create, organize, and develop a large set of possible features for our team’s robotics project, then combine the strongest ideas into three distinct product concepts that visually demonstrate how our design could meet the project’s user needs and technical requirements.

docs.title: Our Ideas
docs.text: Unsorted Categorized

docs.title: How We Chose Our Concept
docs.text:
We arrived at our final concept by combining ideas rather than picking a single one.

  1. Starting point: a motor driver. Our first direction was a DC motor driver with integrated brake chopper and regenerative-braking protection. As we planned the work, we realized a motor driver alone would not give five team members enough meaningful work to divide. Each of us needed a distinct subsystem to design.
  2. Building on the idea. Instead of dropping the motor driver, we made it one part of a larger system. We asked what product needs a reliable motor driver and enough other subsystems for the whole team. That led us to OpenField, an autonomous construction layout robot. The motor driver became the drive subsystem, alongside a master controller, LiDAR obstacle detection, cliff sensing, and a spray marking system.
  3. Learning from existing products. We studied commercial layout robots, including HP SitePrint and Dusty Robotics' FieldPrinter. Both show the value of automated layout, but they are expensive, closed systems. This shaped our goal of an open-source, affordable alternative.
  4. Choosing the drivetrain. We chose treads instead of wheels because they give more traction on rough and loose surfaces such as grass, dirt, and uneven job-site ground, where wheels are more likely to slip. Slipping would throw off where the robot marks.

How the final design differs from our early ideation: Our early brainstorming centered on the motor driver as the whole product. The final design keeps that work as the drive subsystem, and expands the product around it into a complete layout robot with five subsystems, one per team member.

docs.title: How the System Is Connected
docs.text:
OpenField uses a hub-and-spoke layout. One Master board sits in the middle and connects to four subsystem boards, one designed by each team member:

Subsystem Owner Key Components Connection to Master Master Owen C. PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, LCD (UART), dial input Hub: four 8-pin ribbon connectors LiDAR Landon K. PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, ToF LiDAR on a daughter board (UART) UART over Connector 1 Spray Thanh H. PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, servo/solenoid spray actuator (GPIO) UART over Connector 2 Motor Driver Mimi N. PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, left and right motor drivers, two DC motors UART over Connector 3 Cliff Jaedyn H. PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, two LED and sensor pairs for cliff detection UART over Connector 4

Every board talks to the Master over its own UART link (TX/RX) through an 8-contact ribbon cable. Subsystem boards never talk to each other directly. All communication goes through the Master.

docs.title: Why We Structured It This Way
docs.text:
• One board per team member. Each person owns a complete subsystem, from its sensor or actuator to its microcontroller. That gives everyone an equal share of hardware and firmware work, and each board can be built and tested on its own before integration.
  • A single Master makes the decisions. Only the Master combines sensor data and decides when to drive or spray. This keeps the control logic in one place and makes the system easier to debug. It also matches our software proposal, where every board runs the same Read → Think → Output loop.
  • The same microcontroller everywhere. Using the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano on every board means one toolchain and shared code, and boards can be swapped if one fails.
  • Separate UART links on standard connectors. Giving each subsystem its own UART channel avoids bus conflicts between boards. Using the same 8-pin ribbon connector for every board keeps the wiring consistent and lets subsystems be unplugged and replaced easily.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page describes the planned logical behavior of the software running on each microcontroller in our system. Each subsystem has its own activity diagram, created by the team member responsible for it. The Master board coordinates the subsystems: it reads data from the LiDAR and cliff sensors, decides what to do, and then commands the motor driver and the spray system.

Subsystem Owner Role Master Owen C. Starts the system, collects sensor data, and decides on motor and spray actions LiDAR Landon K. Reads the LiDAR sensor and reports obstacle values to the Master Cliff Jaedyn H. Checks for drop-offs and reports clearance to the Master Motor Driver (MD) Mimi N. Compares current and target position and drives the motor Spray Thanh H. Turns the sprayer on and off when signaled

docs.title: Software Diagram
docs.text:
Figure 1: UML activity diagrams for the Master, LiDAR, Cliff, Motor Driver, and Spray microcontrollers. Click the image to enlarge.

Diagram source file: SoftwareProposal.drawio (open it with draw.io using File → Open from → Device).

docs.title: Master
docs.text:
• Main: After it starts, the Master initializes and then runs a continuous Read → Think → Output loop.
  • Initialize: Turns on the HMI and establishes communication with the other boards. If initialization succeeds, it enters a ready state and starts up. If it fails, it enters an error state.
  • Read: Collects the LiDAR string, the cliff sensor value, and the current motor position (Y).
  • Think: Turns the LiDAR and cliff readings into true/false conditions. When both conditions are met, it sets the motor output value and actuates the spray.

docs.title: LiDAR
docs.text:
• Main: Initializes and then loops through Read → Think → Output.
  • Read: Establishes communication with the LiDAR and repeatedly stores incoming LiDAR data.
  • Think: Evaluates the LiDAR data as true or false and stores the resulting obstacle value.
  • Output: Sends the obstacle value to the Master.

docs.title: Cliff
docs.text: After start-up, the cliff board sends a signal and runs a clearance check. The result (true or false) is sent as the output, and the board loops back to send the next signal.

docs.title: Motor Driver (MD)
docs.text: The motor driver reads the commanded position, compares the current position (x) with the target (y), and uses encoder output to keep updating that comparison. When the positions differ, it executes the move. It breaks out of the move once the target is reached, then loops back to read the next command.

docs.title: Spray
docs.text: After start-up and initialization, the spray board waits for a signal from the Master. When the signal is true, it turns the sprayer on and keeps checking whether the signal is still active. When the signal goes false, it turns the sprayer off and returns to waiting for the next signal.

docs.title: Why We Structured the Software This Way
docs.text:
• One diagram per microcontroller. Our block diagram has five boards, so the software has five diagrams. Each team member designed the software for the board they own, which lets everyone develop and test their firmware separately before integration.
  • The same Read → Think → Output loop on every board. Using one common structure makes every board's code predictable and easy to review. It also means the same debugging approach works on every board.
  • Every board loops forever. No diagram ends in a dead end. After each pass, each board returns to the start of its loop, so the robot keeps working without a power cycle, and a board can recover from a bad reading on its next pass.
  • Decisions are made in one place. Subsystem boards only report data (LiDAR, Cliff) or carry out commands (Motor Driver, Spray). Only the Master combines the sensor results and decides what to do. This keeps the safety logic in one place instead of spread across five boards.
  • Safety checks before action. The Master only drives and sprays when both the LiDAR and Cliff checks are clear. If either check fails, the robot does not move or mark.
  • Safe start-up. The Master confirms communication with the other boards during initialization. If that fails, it goes to an error state instead of driving with missing information.

docs.title: How the Software Meets Our Product Needs
docs.text: Product need (from User Needs) How the software handles it Detect and avoid obstacles (needs #1, #60) The LiDAR board checks for obstacles on every loop, and the Master stops motion when one is detected. Detect cliff edges to prevent fall-offs (need #65) The Cliff board runs a clearance check on every loop, and the Master only drives when it is clear. Place marks accurately (need #21) The Motor Driver compares current and target position using encoder feedback until the target is reached. Prevent spills and stray marks (need #29) The Spray board only sprays while the Master's signal is active, and turns off as soon as it ends. Clear diagnostic feedback when a fault occurs (need #58) The Master enters an error state if communication fails during start-up. Recover from communication problems (need #55) Every board loops continuously, so a missed reading is replaced on the next pass.

docs.title: Project Objective
docs.text: Objective: Build a working prototype of OpenField, an open-source autonomous robot that drives over a construction floor or job site and sprays layout marks where the plan says they belong. The prototype should show that an affordable, modular robot can mark a layout safely and repeatably, as a low-cost alternative to commercial layout robots that cost tens of thousands of dollars.

docs.title: Stakeholders
docs.text:
Stakeholder What they need from OpenField Operators (layout crews, builders) A robot that is quick to set up, marks accurately, and is safe to run around other workers. Maintainers Modular parts that are easy to diagnose, swap, and reprint. Firmware Leads Open, well-documented firmware they can extend. Hardware Leads Standard connectors, off-the-shelf parts, and published design files. Construction companies (buyers) A much lower cost than commercial layout robots, with no subscription.

See User Needs and Benchmarking for where each stakeholder's voice came from.

docs.title: Use Case 1: Marking wall lines on a new home's slab
docs.text:
1. A layout crew member carries OpenField onto a finished concrete slab and sets it at the starting point.
  2. The operator powers it on. The Master board starts every subsystem and shows Ready on the LCD. If a board does not respond, the LCD shows an error instead.
  3. The operator uses the dial to start the layout.
  4. OpenField drives along the planned lines. The LiDAR board watches for obstacles, and the Cliff board watches for drop-offs, such as an open stairwell.
  5. While the robot is on a planned line, the Master tells the Spray board to mark the floor.
  6. If a worker steps in front of the robot, it stops and waits. It continues once the path is clear.
  7. When the layout is done, the LCD shows Complete, and the crew starts framing walls on the marked lines.

docs.title: Use Case 2: Marking on rough ground before the slab is poured
docs.text:
1. A crew needs reference marks on a graded dirt or grass site, before the foundation is poured.
  2. OpenField's treads keep traction on loose and uneven ground, where a wheeled robot would slip.
  3. The robot marks the planned points while the Cliff board keeps it away from trenches and excavation edges.
  4. At the end of the day, a maintainer finds the spray actuator worn. Because each subsystem plugs into the Master with the same ribbon connector, they unplug the Spray board, replace the part, and plug it back in without touching the other boards.

docs.title: Hardware / Product Design
docs.text:
• Tracked (tread) chassis for traction on concrete, dirt, gravel, and grass.
  • Five PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano boards: a Master plus LiDAR, Cliff, Motor Driver, and Spray subsystems (see the Team Block Diagram).
  • Each subsystem connects to the Master through an 8-pin ribbon cable.
  • 3D-printed body parts with off-the-shelf fasteners.

docs.title: Software / Functionality
docs.text:
• Every board runs a continuous Read → Think → Output loop (see the Software Proposal).
  • Only the Master makes decisions. Subsystem boards report sensor data or carry out commands.
  • The robot only drives and sprays when the LiDAR and Cliff checks are both clear.

docs.title: Interactivity and User Experience
docs.text:
• An LCD shows the robot's state (ready, running, complete, error) and low-battery warnings.
  • A dial lets the operator start, pause, and select options without a laptop.
  • Clear error messages tell the operator which subsystem has a problem.

docs.title: Customization
docs.text:
• Open-source firmware and design files, so users can change behavior or add features.
  • Modular subsystem boards on standard connectors, so new tools (such as a different marker) can be swapped in.

docs.title: Manufacturing
docs.text:
• Off-the-shelf development boards, sensors, and fasteners.
  • 3D-printed parts that can be reprinted when broken.
  • Design files published so others can build their own.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Obstacle detection with the LiDAR, and drop-off detection with the cliff sensors.
  • An emergency stop that halts all motion and spraying.
  • Safe start-up: the robot will not move if any subsystem fails to respond.
  • The sprayer only runs while the Master's signal is active.

docs.title: Requirement Criteria Specifications
docs.text:
Each requirement has a measurable target, the user need it comes from, and how we will verify it. Need numbers (#) refer to our 75 user needs, and B-numbers refer to needs found in benchmarking.

Verification methods: Test (measured trial), Demonstration (shown working), Inspection (checked by looking or measuring), Analysis (calculated or checked against datasheets).

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
ID Requirement Target Source Need Verification PR-1 Marking accuracy Each mark within ±3 cm of its planned position over a 3 m × 3 m test area #21, B23 Test: Mark 10 planned points, then measure each one's error from the reference with a tape measure. PR-2 Battery runtime At least 4 hours of continuous operation #31 Test: Run continuously from a full charge until shutdown. PR-3 Low-battery warning LCD warning at or below 20% battery #35 Demonstration: Run the battery down and confirm the warning appears.

Why ±3 cm: Commercial layout robots reach 1/16 inch (about 1.6 mm), but they rely on laser trackers or robotic total stations that cost thousands of dollars (benchmarking). Our prototype positions itself with LiDAR and motor encoders, so ±3 cm is a realistic target for this stage. Reaching the 1/16-inch tolerance in need #21 remains a long-term goal.

docs.title: Mobility
docs.text: ID Requirement Target Source Need Verification PR-4 Climb inclines Drives up slopes of at least 2.5° without slipping #14 Test: Drive up a ramp set to 2.5°. PR-5 Cross rough floors Drives over bumps up to 2 cm high #15 Test: Drive over a 2 cm board. PR-6 Fit through doorways Total width of 30 in (76 cm) or less #42 Inspection: Measure the robot's width. PR-7 One-person carry Total weight of 50 lb (22.7 kg) or less #43 Inspection: Weigh the robot.

docs.title: Environmental
docs.text: ID Requirement Target Source Need Verification PR-8 Operating temperature Operates from 14 °F to 122 °F (−10 °C to 50 °C) #12, B14 Analysis: Check every component's rated temperature range on its datasheet.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: ID Requirement Target Source Need Verification PR-9 Obstacle stop Stops at least 30 cm before an obstacle in its path #1, #60 Test: Place an object in the path, 10 trials. Measure the stopping distance each time. PR-10 Drop-off stop Stops before any drop of more than 5 cm, with no part of the treads past the edge #3, #65 Test: Drive toward a table edge, 10 trials. PR-11 Emergency stop Halts all motion and spraying within 1 second #61 Test: Press the stop and time how long it takes the robot to halt. PR-12 Spray control Sprayer turns off within 0.5 seconds after the Master's spray signal ends #29 Test: Time the delay between the signal ending and the spray stopping. PR-13 Safe start-up Robot does not move if any subsystem fails to respond during start-up #64 Demonstration: Unplug one board before power-on, and confirm the robot stays still and shows an error.

docs.title: Software and Communication
docs.text: ID Requirement Target Source Need Verification PR-14 Detect lost boards Master detects a disconnected subsystem within 1 second and names it on the LCD #55, #58 Demonstration: Unplug a ribbon cable during operation. PR-15 Status display LCD shows the current state: ready, running, complete, or error #56, #62 Demonstration: Step through each state.

docs.title: Manufacturing and Customization
docs.text: ID Requirement Target Source Need Verification PR-16 Standard parts All fasteners are standard off-the-shelf sizes, and all custom parts can be 3D printed #68, #71 Inspection: Review the bill of materials. PR-17 Swappable subsystems Any subsystem board can be unplugged and replaced in under 5 minutes without tools #50, #70 Test: Time a board swap. PR-18 Open source Firmware and design files are published on GitHub #75 Inspection: Check the public repositories.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
1. Positioning: Can LiDAR and motor encoders alone hold ±3 cm over a full layout, or will we need extra reference markers or a total station?
  2. Tread slip: How much do the treads slip on smooth concrete, and how much does that hurt accuracy?
  3. Marking medium: Which spray paint or marker works best on both concrete and dirt, and how do we keep it from clogging?
  4. Loading the plan: How will layouts get onto the robot? Right now, the operator only has the LCD and dial.
  5. Power: What battery type and capacity do we need to reach 4 hours, given the motors' current draw? Each teammate's power budget will help answer this.
  6. Cost: What is a realistic total parts cost for the prototype?
